items.title: Why the gap shrinks
items.prose: Take any rule $u_{n+1} = au_n + b$ with $a \ne 1$, and let $L$ be the value it leaves alone. Show when the terms close in on $L$.
items.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: $L = aL + b$, since the rule leaves $L$ alone
$u_{n+1} - L = (au_n + b) - (aL + b)$, the rule minus that equation
$u_{n+1} - L = a(u_n - L)$, the $b$ terms cancel and $a$ factors out
So the gaps $u_n - L$ form a geometric sequence with ratio $a$
If $-1 < a < 1$, then $a^{n-1}$ shrinks towards 0, so $u_n$ closes in on $L$

items.title: An account that drains
items.prompt:
A trading account holds £10,000.00. Each month it earns 1% on its balance, then £120.00 is withdrawn.

(a) Write a recurrence relation for the balance $B_n$ after $n$ months, with its starting value.

(b) Compute $B_1$, $B_2$ and $B_3$ to the penny.

(c) Find the balance $L$ that the rule leaves alone. Say whether this account moves towards $L$ or away from it, and why.

(d) Show that the gap $B_n - L$ is geometric, write $B_n$ as a formula in $n$, and use it to find $B_{12}$.

(e) What monthly withdrawal would keep the balance at £10,000.00 for ever?
items.model:
**(a)** Each month multiplies by 1.01, then subtracts 120: $B_{n+1} = 1.01B_n - 120$, with $B_0 = 10000$.

**(b)** $B_1 = 1.01 \times 10000 - 120 = 9980.00$. $B_2 = 1.01 \times 9980 - 120 = 9959.80$. $B_3 = 1.01 \times 9959.80 - 120 = 9939.398$, so £9,939.40.

**(c)** $L = 1.01L - 120$ gives $0.01L = 120$, so $L = 12000$. At £12,000.00 the interest, £120.00, exactly covers the withdrawal. This account starts £2,000.00 below $L$. Each month multiplies that gap by 1.01, so the gap grows and the balance falls away from $L$, ever faster.

**(d)** Subtracting $L = 1.01L - 120$ from the rule gives $B_{n+1} - 12000 = 1.01(B_n - 12000)$. So the gaps are geometric with ratio 1.01 and first value $B_0 - 12000 = -2000$. Hence $B_n - 12000 = -2000 \times 1.01^n$, so $B_n = 12000 - 2000 \times 1.01^n$. Then $B_{12} = 12000 - 2000 \times 1.01^{12} \approx 12000 - 2253.65 = 9746.35$, so £9,746.35.

**(e)** The balance stays put when the withdrawal equals the interest: 1% of £10,000.00, which is £100.00. Check: $1.01 \times 10000 - 100 = 10000$.

rubric.text: Gives £9,980.00, £9,959.80 and £9,939.40, applying the interest before the withdrawal.
Solves $L = 1.01L - 120$ for £12,000.00 and explains that the gap grows by a factor of 1.01, so the balance falls away.
Shows $B_{n+1} - L = 1.01(B_n - L)$, writes $B_n = 12000 - 2000 \times 1.01^n$ and gives $B_{12} \approx$ £9,746.35.
Gives £100.00, as the withdrawal that equals the monthly interest, with a check.
